title_en: US reportedly strikes Iran’s Qeshm Island as Vance voices optimism about a deal
excerpt_en: Iranian state media reported the sound of explosions on the island in the strait of Hormuz, coming on the eve of crucial US midterms
body_en: The ⁠US launched limited strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island late on Monday, ⁠according to reports in US media, hours after US vice-president JD Vance said he was optimistic diplomatic efforts to end the war were moving in the right direction.

The strikes were reported as being “defensive”, and not thought to be a signal of a return to full hostilities, but came on the eve of crucial midterm elections in which Donald Trump’s Republican party is expected to be punished by voters for the cascading effect the war has had on the US cost of living.
When asked earlier on Monday whether he had considered resuming strikes on Iran after Tuesday’s midterm elections, Trump replied “no”.
Related: Oil price falls amid hope of a breakthrough to end Iran war

Several explosions were ⁠heard ⁠on Qeshm Island on Monday evening, according to Iranian state media, with local outlets describing their cause as unclear. The strikes – first reported by the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) – targeted surface to air missiles being used against US assets, according to Reuters and the Associated Press.

US Central ‌Command did not immediately ⁠respond to a request for comment from the Reuters news agency, and the WSJ described the attacks as part of a series of strikes carried out against the country in recent weeks that have not been made public.

The paper said that sources suggested the recent strikes have been carried out on a smaller scale and purposefully kept secret by the Trump administration so as not to signal ‌any intent of resuming the military campaign against Iran.

The US has targeted Qeshm Island on multiple occasions throughout the war. Positioned in the mouth of the strait of Hormuz, the island has been used in the past to launch attacks on shipping in the waterway.

Despite attacks having ceased in recent weeks, Iran has continued to enforce its closure of the strait by targeting oil tankers, shipping containers and other vessels attempting to transit the waterway.

If confirmed, the attack would mark the first publicly known strike by the US on Iran in weeks. On Monday Vance said that he and Trump were optimistic about securing a deal with Iran, after Tehran revealed indirect negotiations with Washington.

“The president and I both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement,” Vance told reporters. “We’ve certainly made some progress. We’ll see if we can make some more.”
Speaking to Fox News hours before the polls opened in the US on Tuesday, Trump continued to play down the significance of the conflict and its effects on the US economy.
“There’s no war raging. It could happen if they don’t make a deal, but they want to make a deal very badly and there’s a very good chance we make a deal.”

Speaking from Washington in his closing message of the midterms campaign, Trump hailed a sharp drop in oil prices that came as his administration touted a renewed diplomatic efforts being made to end the war. Rising petrol prices have caused by the war have become a signature issue of the midterm elections, with polls showing voters likely to punish Republicans for the effect on the cost of living.

title_en: After ProPublica Investigation, House Democrats Demand Answers on U.S. Citizens Detained by Immigration Agents
excerpt_en: The post After ProPublica Investigation, House Democrats Demand Answers on U.S. Citizens Detained by Immigration Agents appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: Photo illustration by ProPublica. Source images: Congress and videos obtained by ProPublica. What Happened: Citing ProPublica’s recent investigation, House Democrats are again asking the Trump administration to explain why hundreds of U.S. citizens have been held by immigration agents and how the government verifies citizenship during immigration operations.

In an October letter to Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, California Rep. Lou Correa and 39 other legislators demanded the administration share the number of citizens that immigration agents have detained and how the government is tracking such encounters. They also asked for more information about how agents are trained to verify citizenship and legal status.
Why It Matters: ProPublica counted more than 500 Americans detained by immigration agents — almost certainly an undercount since the government is not transparently tracking the cases.

Experts told us the cases collectively show federal agents running roughshod over the constitutional rights of citizens. We found more than 100 Americans who were questioned about their citizenship, 63 Americans detained while recording, 36 Americans held for at least a day without being able to contact a lawyer or their family and roughly a dozen citizens deported, mostly children.

What They Said: “We remain concerned that the Department’s actions are violating American citizens’ constitutional rights to due process, equal protection, and freedom from unreasonable search and seizure, and request transparency regarding the Department’s actions,” the representatives wrote in their letter to DHS.
DHS has long insisted it is not arresting U.S. citizens, and it defended its immigration operations as “highly targeted.”

“These members of Congress have shown more concern for criminal illegal aliens who’ve broken our laws and destroyed any possibility of ever remaining in our country than they ever have for Rachel Morin, Laken Riley, Jocelyn Nungaray, and the true victims of illegal alien crimes in America,” a spokesperson wrote to ProPublica.

Background: Democrats have been pushing the second Trump administration for more details about how immigration agents are interacting with U.S. citizens since early 2025. Last year, congressional Democrats announced a wide-ranging investigation into immigration agents’ detention of U.S. citizens in response to our earlier reporting that found that more than 170 citizens were detained by immigration agents.

Last month, Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, a New Mexico Democrat, introduced a bill, Justice for Citizens Wrongfully Detained by ICE Act, that would make it easier for citizens to sue immigration agents for wrongful arrests.

More Than 500 U.S. Citizens Have Been Detained, Including Handcuffed or Held at Gunpoint, in Trump’s Immigration Crackdown The post After ProPublica Investigation, House Democrats Demand Answers on U.S. Citizens Detained by Immigration Agents appeared first on ProPublica.

title_en: When a bull falls for a donkey: what an unlikely relationship reveals about animal sexuality
excerpt_en: Same-sex behaviour is common in animals, but a bull and a male donkey in Ethiopia are an unusual pair. What might they tell us about sex in nature?
body_en: Achille with Patroclo. Andre B da Cruz UNIPI, CC BY On an Ethiopian plateau, a bull called Achille formed an unusual relationship with a male donkey named Patroclo. They were observed spending time together, licking and rubbing against one another, and repeatedly having penetrative sex.

The animals’ names nod to Achilles and Patroclus, the Greek mythological figures whose bond has been debated for thousands of years: devoted friends – or lovers? A new study in the journal Current Biology asks something similar about Achille and Patroclo: why would two males of different species repeatedly choose each other as sexual partners when females of their own species are available?
Perhaps the more interesting question is why we find their relationship so surprising.
A chance find The researchers first noticed Achille and Patroclo while studying gelada monkeys in Ethiopia. Intrigued, they began observing the pair more closely.

They recorded 51 mounting attempts, 34 of which involved penetration. Patroclo took an active role, presenting his hindquarters to Achille and initiating contact. Unlike another male donkey that Achille approached, Patroclo did not show obvious signs of trying to avoid him.
The donkey and bull often showed affection towards each other immediately after mounting. This suggests that sex may help strengthen their bond.

The researchers observed the pair in detail for just four days, so they cannot say how long the relationship lasted. Even so, the findings are unusual because the two animals are both male and belong to different species.

Same-sex sexual behaviour has been reported in more than 1,500 animal species. A 2023 study documented it in 261 mammalian species and found that it was particularly associated with social species, suggesting a possible role in maintaining relationships and managing conflict.

As a primatologist, I am not surprised by these findings. Bonobos, for example, are famous for their frequent sexual interactions, which occur in many combinations of partners. Female–female genital rubbing, for instance, is associated with affiliation and social bonding. Sexual interactions can also help manage social tensions.

Same-sex sexual behaviour takes many forms. Male bottlenose dolphins mount one another and rub genitals in groups that cooperate to gain access to females, while female Japanese macaques form temporary sexual partnerships involving repeated mounting. Same-sex sexual behaviour may play a part in establishing status, settling disputes, forming friendships or sexual enjoyment.

Sexual behaviour between different species is rarer, but it is not unheard of. Both male and female Japanese macaques, for example, mount sika deer. Unlike the apparently reciprocal relationship between Achille and Patroclo, these encounters do not necessarily involve mutual sexual interest.
What makes Achille and Patroclo particularly interesting is that they combine sexual activity with apparent affection and a preference for each other.

Evolutionary biologists have traditionally approached same-sex sexual behaviour as a puzzle. If natural selection favours traits that contribute to reproductive success, why should animals spend time and energy engaging in sexual behaviour that cannot directly produce offspring?

Suggested explanations include mistaken identity, a lack of opposite-sex partners, or indiscriminate sexual behaviour with whichever individuals happen to be nearby. But all these explanations begin with an assumption that sexual behaviour between males and females is the default, and same-sex behaviour represents a departure from it.

In a provocative 2019 paper, a team of researchers challenged this assumption. They proposed that the ancestors of sexually reproducing animals may have been relatively indiscriminate about the sex of their sexual partners. Rather than assuming that different-sex sexual behaviour came first, they suggested that the ability to distinguish between potential partners, and preferentially direct sexual behaviour towards the opposite sex, may have evolved later.
Taking a queer perspective This is a brilliant example of how queer perspectives can enrich evolutionary biology.

Queer approaches encourage scientists to examine how human assumptions about sex, gender and sexuality influence the questions we ask, the categories we use and the explanations we consider plausible. They do not require us to assign human sexual identities to animals.

Observing same-sex sexual behaviour does not tell us that an animal is gay or establish a fixed sexual orientation. Instead, queer approaches encourage us to take the diversity of animal sexual behaviour seriously, without assuming what is normal or what needs explaining.

The authors of the new study suggest that Achille and Patroclo’s sexual interactions may help maintain their social relationship. They also discuss the possible reproductive costs of spending time and energy on sexual activity that cannot result in offspring.
But this framing raises another question. Why should we assume that sexual behaviour must contribute directly to reproduction to have evolutionary significance?

Social relationships can influence survival, access to resources and future reproductive opportunities. Sexual behaviour that strengthens those relationships may therefore have adaptive benefits, even when it cannot directly produce offspring. Equally, sexual behaviour may arise from evolved mechanisms without every individual encounter necessarily providing an animal’s reproductive success.

Achille and Patroclo cannot tell us why they choose one another. This short study can’t tell us what evolutionary purpose, if any, their relationship serves. But it does remind us that animal behaviour can be more diverse than our theories suggest.

title_en: AI-powered malware ‘highly likely’ to be used to hack UK infrastructure by 2028
excerpt_en: National Cyber Security Centre expects attacks on critical facilities such as power stations, airports and hospitals
body_en: AI-powered malicious software is “highly likely” to be used in hacking attacks against the UK’s power stations, airports and hospitals by 2028, according to the state cybersecurity body.

The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) said AI will probably enable a ransomware attack against critical national infrastructure [CNI] between now and 2028. The UK’s definition of CNI covers a range of facilities and services across sectors including energy, transport, defence, food, health and finance.
The warning from the NCSC, part of the GCHQ spy agency, was published in the organisation’s annual review, which also warned that Russia and China will start using AI “routinely” in cyber-attacks.
“It is … highly likely that between now and 2028, AI-powered malware will have been used in a ransomware attack on UK CNI,” said NCSC.
Ransomware has become a cornerstone of the criminal hacker’s repertoire and is a signature ploy of gangs that typically operate out of former Soviet Union states.

After gaining access to a victim’s IT systems, the attackers then encrypt files with bespoke malicious software – or malware – and then demand a payment in cryptocurrency to unlock the crippled systems and return any stolen data. UK ransomware victims include Royal Mail, outsourcing firm Capita and various public bodies, including councils.
AI is set to enhance the ransomware threat by helping attackers with tasks such as scouting targets, locating weaknesses in IT networks and writing malicious code, said the NCSC.

Last month, the government urged Britons to stock up to nine litres of bottled water and three days’ worth of food in order to ensure that households can survive a weather, cyber or other serious emergency. Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, said as the Be Ready campaign was launched that Britain needed to prepare for the threat of “state-sponsored terrorism” by Russia or other hostile powers targeting everyday infrastructure.
NCSC’s chief executive, Richard Horne, will warn the public in a speech accompanying the review on Tuesday that AI is going to unleash a wave of cyber-attacks imminently.
“In the coming months, we face a real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents,” he will say.
Horne will attribute the threat to the technology’s ability to uncover weaknesses in IT systems that have been “tolerated for far too long”.

An example of AI’s capacity to root out previously undetected vulnerabilities came last month, when the technology helped discover a critical weakness in PHP, a computer language used by almost 70% of the world’s websites.
Alan Woodward, a professor of cybersecurity at Surrey University, said NCSC’s warning underlined the need for nation states and companies to access cutting-edge AI technology.

“AI can help people find these flaws and patch them, but if we don’t get the access the bad guys will beat them to it,” he said. So far, leading AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic have given some companies advanced access to their most powerful models in order to help them identify serious IT glitches.
Horne will also say in his speech that communications networks used by the British military are subjected to daily attacks that are “persistent” and “sustained”.

Horne will say Russia was one of the perpetrators, but the attacks have deliberately not crossed the line into warfare, with Moscow carrying out “notable campaigns” that “intentionally fall below the threshold of armed conflict as they escalate their attempts at hybrid warfare”.

Horne will add that recent cyber-attacks on supermarket fridges in Europe, which have seen fridge temperatures raised by hackers to more than 50C, are a warning to companies and organisations to invest strongly in cyber resilience.
“For decades we have collectively got away with tech on the cheap,” he will say.

title_en: Fossilised red blood cells found in 115m-year-old dinosaur’s bone, say scientists
excerpt_en: Chemical tests on Aratasaurus bone identify presence of heme, the organic compound that allows haemoglobin in blood to carry oxygen around body
body_en: It could be the opening of a Jurassic Park rip-off: scientists examining ancient dinosaur bones find what appear to be fossilised red blood cells, and traces of the molecule that gives the beast’s blood its distinctive crimson hue.

But that is what researchers are claiming to have discovered after analysing the hind leg bones of a small, meat-eating dinosaur called an Aratasaurus that lived and died in what is now north-eastern Brazil 115m years ago.

Electron microscope images of the dinosaur bones revealed small, round structures that resemble red blood cells in fine channels where blood vessels once ran, while chemical tests identified the presence of heme, the organic compound that allows haemoglobin in blood to carry oxygen around the body.

Such claims are controversial because biological tissues and molecules can break down fast, leaving little or no trace in ancient fossils. But if confirmed, it would open up entirely new avenues for scientists, allowing them to investigate dinosaur blood, metabolism and even their activity levels.

“We are seeing a mineral and molecular echo of the dinosaur’s original biology,” said Prof Kliti Grice at Curtin University in Western Australia who led the research team. “Fossilised red blood cells with distinct chemistry related to heme have never been found in situ in any fossil, let alone a dinosaur. This is a world first.”

The fossilised remnants of the Aratasaurus were discovered in a mine in 2008 and have since been held in the National Museum of Brazil, where researchers continue to study them. While analysing the dinosaur’s hind leg bones, Grice spotted the structures that resembled red blood cells.

The scientists’ suspicions that they were looking at red blood cells were bolstered when chemical tests came back positive for heme and its breakdown products. Tests also found traces of the amino acid building blocks for collagen, a key protein in connective and other tissues.

If the structures really are fossilised red blood cells, as the researchers contend, it raises the question of how they were preserved. According to Grice, a manganese compound called hausmannite, which formed in and around the blood cells, may have lent a helping hand by stabilising them prior to fossilisation. The same process might have helped preserve the amino acids, she added. The study appears in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

The work is already stoking debate. Prof Mary Schweitzer at North Carolina State University in the US, who has discovered remnants of blood vessels and soft tissues in dinosaur fossils, is not convinced Grice and her colleagues have found red blood cells. One reason for her doubt is that the dinosaur’s red blood cells should have a “nuclear bulge” making them appear dome-like on both sides. The structures Grice found are concave, suggesting they might be something else.

Schweitzer was more persuaded by the discovery of heme and collagen amino acids in the bone and said there was so much more to learn from exceptionally well-preserved fossils. Schweitzer added: “The conventional wisdom in palaeontology that all endogenous organics would disappear in a million years or less is being routinely challenged, and will continue to be as technological approaches to palaeontological specimens are more routinely applied.”

Another question the research raises is what other biological material might lurk in fossils collections around the world. On this, Grice urges extreme caution, adding that her work does not imply that large biological molecules such as proteins or DNA live on in ancient fossils. “Any extraordinary claim needs extraordinary analytical evidence,” she said. “The aim isn’t to find Jurassic Park DNA, it’s to determine how much genuine molecular information deep time can preserve.”

“The really exciting implication is that extraordinary molecular information may already be sitting in museum collections around the world, waiting for us to ask new questions of old fossils,” she added.

title_en: “Chaos” in the Air: Five Ways Voting Could Be Disrupted on Election Day
excerpt_en: The post “Chaos” in the Air: Five Ways Voting Could Be Disrupted on Election Day appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: Election workers in Los Angeles County process ballots for the state’s primary in June. Mario Tama/Getty Images As Americans head to the polls on Tuesday, voting experts are watching to see how the Trump administration’s unprecedented efforts to assert more federal control over elections will play out.

Since President Donald Trump retook the White House, his administration has tried to force states to turn over their unredacted voter rolls and to restrict mail-in voting. The Department of Homeland Security has used its resources to identify and prosecute noncitizen voters, an effort that has unfolded alongside the agency’s massive crackdown on immigrants.
The president has justified these steps by claiming, without evidence, that American elections are beset by fraud and that illegal voting is tipping the scales in favor of Democrats.

Help Us Report on Key Election Issues ProPublica’s reporters are on the lookout for what’s going right and what isn’t. We’re monitoring voter suppression and interference, election observers and poll watchers, extremism tied to the election, and ICE activity at the polls. Have you seen something?

Send Us a Tip Courts have thwarted most of the administration’s plans to date, but Trump and his top deputies have kept up the pressure. Most recently, they’ve threatened to prosecute election officials who don’t reject ballots from people that the federal government has identified as likely noncitizens.
The administration hasn’t explicitly ruled out sending federal agents to the polls or seizing ballots or voting machines.
Election experts say the cumulative effect has been to ramp up anxiety about the midterms and to erode voters’ trust in the system.

“The administration has been creating a lot of noise, a lot of confusion, a lot of doubt,” said Ben Hovland, whom Trump fired as a commissioner for the bipartisan Election Assistance Commission earlier this year. He said he worries that this will make voters “sit it out” and “throw their hands up.”
“Paper Trail” Podcast Learn more about this story on ProPublica’s podcast “ Paper Trail.”

In an emailed response to questions, a DHS spokesperson said Immigration and Customs Enforcement “is not planning operations targeting polling locations,” adding that the agency would only arrest people at the polls to address a safety threat as part of “intelligence-driven targeted enforcement.”

The DHS and the Justice Department “are laser focused on identifying, prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S. citizens,” the spokesperson added. “Our message to aliens who vote in American elections is clear: we will find you, arrest you, and you will face the consequences — including criminal charges and deportation.”

Before and on Election Day, it’s typical for the major political parties to mount poll-watching operations, but both Democrats and Republicans say they’ve expanded these activities in this pressurized midterm.

Republicans will focus on issues such as voter eligibility and voter-roll accuracy, according to Ally Triolo, the Republican National Committee’s election integrity communications director. Democrats will concentrate on voter intimidation and other hurdles to voting, Angelo Fernández Hernández, a Democratic National Committee spokesperson, said.
Here are five issues that voting rights experts say they’re watching as this year’s election unfolds:

People arrive to vote early on Oct. 27 in Coral Gables, Florida. Lynne Sladky/AP Images 1. Will There Be Federal Interference? An incident in Leon County, in the Florida Panhandle, illustrates the widespread anxiety about law enforcement at the polls.

Mark Earley, the county’s supervisor of elections, told ProPublica he was “furious” when two marked U.S. Customs and Border Protection vehicles parked outside the county’s busiest early voting location last month, after he’d been repeatedly reassured by the administration that agents would not do this.
He reported the sighting to the FBI, then learned that the agents, who were headed out of state, had just stopped by to try to vote themselves. The episode generated a flurry of news coverage.
“Given the negative media coverage regarding federal agents at the polls, it shows pretty bad judgment that they showed up in their official vehicles,” Earley said.
It’s against the law for federal law enforcement to be near polling places.

Nick Brown, Washington’s attorney general, leads a group of Democratic state officials and voting rights advocates who have been planning how to respond if, indeed, there is real federal interference. The group has “war-gamed” how to react if government agents attempt to commandeer voting equipment or ballots.
“We’ve seen the tension and chaos that’s in the air,” Brown said. He called the federal government “the biggest challenge to smooth elections right now, which is not the way it’s supposed to be.”
A DOJ spokesperson said “the best preparation for any election official is following federal law.”

title_en: Control of Britain’s 39m smart meters passes to non-profit startup
excerpt_en: The handover marks the end of a 13-year licence for Smart DCC, a subsidiary of Capita, after years of spiralling costs and delays
body_en: Control over Great Britain’s 39m smart meters has passed to a non-profit startup after its former owner presided over more than a decade of spiralling costs and delays in the troubled network.

The company owned by crisis-hit outsourcing firm Capita has promised a “seamless transition” to its not-for-profit successor, which will take over running the data network connecting the smart meters from this week.

The handover marks the end of a 13-year licence granted to Smart DCC, a subsidiary of Capita, to set up the country’s first smart meter data network, a process that has been dogged by costly delays while millions of households faced billing issues.

Industry sources said Capita’s subsidiary was effectively blocked from tendering for a new licence to manage the smart meter network after Whitehall officials decided to replace the commercial framework established in 2013 with a not-for-profit public-interest model governed by an independent board.

Instead, the network underpinning Britain’s smart meters will become a wholly owned subsidiary of the Smart Energy Code Company (SECCo) with “a greater focus on cost, transparency and customer and consumer needs”, the new operator said.

Its board will include veteran energy and telecoms industry executives as well as Dame Gillian Guy, the former chief executive of Citizens Advice, which claimed in 2024 that households had been “let down” by the rollout because almost a third of smart meters weren’t working properly.

Ministers had initially hoped that all households would have a smart meter before 2020 to help modernise Britain’s outdated energy system and make better use of renewable energy and innovative data-led energy tariffs.

But the rollout has faced “serious reputational obstacles”, according to the government’s spending watchdog, which meant that three in 10 households still do not have a meter and another £1.7bn may be required to complete the rollout.

The tender process for a new smart network operator ran last summer, at around the same time that the industry regulator opened an investigation into Smart DCC’s procurement contracts, which included deals that were awarded without a competitive process and one which was granted to its parent company, Capita.

Smart DCC agreed in July to pay £200,000 into a consumer redress fund, in the same week that its parent company was forced to apologise for its role in administering the crisis-hit Civil Service Pension Scheme, which kept thousands of retired civil servants waiting for payments.

Capita’s market value has plunged by 97% in the last decade after the outsourcing company once in charge of administering a string of government schemes revealed severely strained finances and mounting debts before undertaking an emergency restructuring of the business.

A Capita spokesperson said: “Capita is proud of its 13-year stewardship of DCC. What began as an ambitious programme is now critical national infrastructure, connecting more than 39.2m smart meters across 23m homes and small businesses, with network availability of 99.6%.
“We hand over a secure and resilient network that millions of consumers rely on every day and have been working with stakeholders to ensure an orderly transition to DCC’s next chapter.”

A spokesperson for Ofgem said Smart DCC had “played a critical role” in delivering “an efficient and secure digital communication structure”, and that the new licence holder would be expected to “build on that solid foundation”.

title_en: Tribal Leaders Warned Border Wall Construction Would Disturb Native American Remains. They Were Right.
excerpt_en: The post Tribal Leaders Warned Border Wall Construction Would Disturb Native American Remains. They Were Right. appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: Quitobaquito Springs, a rare Sonoran Desert oasis imperiled by border wall construction, is located within 200 feet of the U.S.-Mexico border in Organ Pipe National Monument outside Ajo, Arizona. Anna Watts Lorraine Eiler stood in the blazing August sun, surrounded by reporters, to offer a warning. The Trump administration was racing to erect a second border wall across Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument, southwest of Tucson. If the bulldozers came, she said, they were bound to disturb the final resting places of her family and Hia-Ced O’odham tribal ancestors.
“People used to live here,” the 89-year-old said.
Fifteen days later, her fears were realized.
ProPublica has confirmed that Native American remains were unearthed in Organ Pipe amid soil overturned by border wall contractors.

The discovery, unreported until now, was made on Sept. 8, the National Park Service said in a statement. “Following established protocols, the University of Arizona conducted an assessment and confirmed that the remains are human and align with tribal cremation practices,” the agency said.

The Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act governs the steps agencies must take following an inadvertent discovery of Native American remains on federal land. Those steps include halting any activity that contributed to the discovery until tribal communities are consulted.

“The National Park Service is committed to respecting tribal rights and traditions,” the agency went on to say, adding that it was “working diligently to identify the culturally affiliated tribe and ensure the respectful return of the remains, so the tribe may observe their religious and cultural practices.”

Eiler was alerted to the discovery by a cultural affairs specialist with the Tohono O’odham Nation, a larger tribe whose reservation is east of Organ Pipe, and later by the Organ Pipe superintendent’s office. Her family discussed what to do next. Ultimately, they decided to hold off on reburying the newly unearthed remains until construction in the area stops, fearing the work will disturb more sites.
“Who knows what more will come up,” Eiler said in an interview. “They’re going to find remains wherever they dig.”

Hia-Ced O’odham elder Lorraine Eiler stands in the shade of a giant saguaro cactus in Organ Pipe National Monument in 2022. Roberto “Bear” Guerra Customs and Border Protection contractors have bulldozed a wide swath of vegetation parallel to the international divide. The agency has fashioned staging areas for heavy equipment by knocking down, uprooting and attempting to transplant select specimens of the monument’s native plants. Eiler was told the remains were found by a park service archaeologist near the base of a saguaro cactus that was still standing.

In a statement, CBP said it was advised of the discovery six days after it was made, that its cultural resource specialists examined the area and found no other remains, and that “no additional construction has occurred at this location to date.”

The discovery comes amid tensions between the Department of Homeland Security and tribal communities in the Sonoran Desert. In April, border wall contractors bulldozed through a large, well-marked earthen etching, known as the Las Playas Intaglio, that was believed to be at least 6,500 years old. (CBP said the incident was accidental.)

Soon after, the department awarded a $1.3 billion contract for construction of a 62-mile border wall across the entirety of the Tohono O’odham Nation. The tribe is fighting the project in federal court and has erected “no trespassing” signs to keep border wall contractors off its land. As ProPublica recently reported, DHS has responded by deploying masked federal agents as escorts for its work crews and conducting aerial surveillance of tribal members. The head of CBP has justified the need for a wall by describing the reservation as “one of the most dangerous smuggling and trafficking corridors on the Southwest border.”
Verlon M. Jose, the tribe’s chairman, expressed gratitude that the park service had notified his office of the discovery, but mourned the fact that it was necessary.

“When you have mass destruction and disturbance of land taking place where there are clearly sacred sites, cemeteries and other areas of cultural importance, these types of discoveries are bound to happen,” Jose said in a statement. “Every time this happens it is a wound to the heart of all members of the Tohono O’odham Nation — these are our ancestors, our family members — whose remains are being desecrated.”

U.S. Rep. Adelita Grijalva, who appeared with Eiler and the chairman at the August news conference, blasted the government for failing to heed their warnings. “Tribal leaders and elders have warned DHS about the devastating consequences of bulldozing through their ancestral lands, beginning with the destruction of the Las Playas Intaglio,” she said in a statement. “For months, those warnings have fallen on deaf ears. Now, we are seeing exactly what they feared: sacred sites destroyed and ancestral burial grounds desecrated.”
James T. Watson, curator of bioarcheology in the Arizona State Museum at the University of Arizona, analyzed the remains recovered in Organ Pipe in the field.

While he was not authorized to discuss the details of his findings without park service approval, Watson said in an email that he confirmed the remains were human. The evidence suggested they were cremated in a manner consistent with precolonial practices in the region dating back 1,500 years, he wrote.

Under NAGPRA, the graves protection act, Native American remains inadvertently uncovered on park service lands must be immediately secured, Watson explained, and the superintendent of the jurisdiction must notify “all relevant lineal descendants” with “potential cultural affiliation or ancestral ties to the land.”

title_en: Brickmaker’s woes deepen the UK housebuilding gloom
excerpt_en: Ibstock has issued a thumping profits warning, with sales 22% below expectations in the third quarter
body_en: With John Healey’s Your First Home scheme on the way, is the mood improving in the housebuilding sector? A couple of the builders have results later this week, so can speak for themselves. In the meantime, though, here’s a thumping profits warning from Ibstock, the country’s biggest brickmaker, to spread a little more gloom. Demand hit a brick wall in the summer, as the company could have put it.

Industry data, said Ibstock, show UK brick market volumes down 17% year-on-year in July and August. For the whole of the third quarter, it said, sales were 22% below expectations, forcing a one-fifth cut in its production volumes versus plans set out as recently as August.

Cue an 11% fall in the share price to virtually its lowest level since the firm relisted on the stock market in 2015. Top-line earnings for the whole of 2026 will be “in the mid-£40m range” versus a figure close to £60m expected by the City.

The short moral from Ibstock’s woes is that the sector’s slowdown is pretty entrenched. Across the board, we’ve heard shareholder-friendly vows from housebuilders of “financial discipline”, corporate-speak for saying expansion is off the table and the job is about hammering away at costs. Berkeley Homes, focused on the south-east of England, even said six months ago it will stop buying new land and hiring new staff.

Everybody knows one deep cause: the turnaround in interest rate expectations with the Iran war. The Bank of England will probably raise rates this week (finally); then we’ll be on to wondering how many more increases will follow. In addition, housebuilders complain about costs of regulation that are harder to lose when the prices of new houses are going sideways.

So is Healey’s Your First Home a reheat of Help to Buy, a gamechanger? From the point of view of housebuilders, the scheme is clearly welcome – they had been lobbying for action for ages. But there are a couple of caveats. First, the caps on the size of the transactions means it is not a copycat scheme for the very good reason that Healey can’t be seen to be adding too much inflationary pressure at a time like now.

Second, it will only be launched next April, the chancellor said in his budget last week. The delay “may weigh on demand in the intervening period”, Ibstock chief executive Joe Hudson said, echoing others. He is surely right: for many qualifying buyers, it will make sense to wait five months for the discounted loans.

Healey also said there will be no more changes to building regulations in this parliament (except where critical for safety), a nod towards the sector’s other grumble. On the other hand, he’s not proposing to remove existing regulations.

So one suspects 2027 – a year of 1% growth in the economy, according to the Office for Budget Responsibility’s forecasts – is probably not going to move housebuilding volumes meaningfully. Your First Home should be “modestly helpful”, reckons Peel Hunt, but “lower interest rates remain key to a pickup in sector activity”. Yes, it all comes back to borrowing costs. And the upturn, when it comes, will surely be too late to save the government’s ambition of 1.5m new homes this parliament. The target isn’t officially rubble, but it may as well be.

title_en: Nearly all Americans believe corruption is a problem. But will it decide the midterm elections?
excerpt_en: The vast majority of Americans believe government corruption is widespread – both Democrats and Republicans. Politicians have taken notice.
body_en: In a politically polarised American electorate, it can be hard to find bipartisan consensus on many issues. Ahead of the US midterm elections, however, there is one thing almost everyone can agree on: concern about government corruption.

A record 89% of Americans recently said in a Gallup poll that government corruption is widespread, with Republicans, Democrats and independents all in agreement (ranging between 83-91%). This marks a significant increase from 73% in Gallup’s polling from 2024.
Out of 132 countries Gallup polled on the question since 2023, only four have recorded higher overall levels of concern: Lebanon and Peru (both 92%), and Ghana and Nigeria (both 90%).

As much as cost of living issues have defined much of the recent campaign rhetoric, a recent Fox News Poll found that concern about corruption in government (88%) ranked higher among voters than inflation (85%) or gas prices (83%).
A CNBC survey similarly found government corruption to be the most important issue facing the country, above any concerns about the economy.

And according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact, of the US$11.6 billion that will be spent in political advertising this election cycle, more than US$275 million has gone to corruption-themed ads – around US$173 for Democrats and US$93 for Republicans.

An ad produced by a Democratic super PAC accusing Republican Maine Senator Susan Collins of corruption. An ad by Republican Minnesota Senate candidate Michele Tafoya accusing Democrats of failing to stop fraud in the state. Who do Americans blame? As much as Democrats point to the unprecedented gifts from foreign governments to the Trump family and the massive expansion of the Trump family wealth during Donald Trump’s second presidential term, Americans are by no means exclusively blaming the Trump administration for corruption.

When the Brennan Center for Justice, a voting rights organisation, asked a representative sample of 2,000 Americans this year whether certain individuals or institutions were corrupt, respondents had negative views across the political spectrum. These included view about Congress (85%), Trump (68%), Joe Biden (63%) and the Supreme Court (62%).

And when asked whether this is a problem driven by individuals making unethical choices or a problem “deeply embedded in the institutions of the US government”, about two-thirds of respondents chose the latter. Only 7% said they were not concerned about corruption influencing elected officials.

This does not appear to be a new phenomenon. Levels of trust in American politicians, political parties, news media, government institutions and even the “American people” have been declining since Gallup began polling on the issue in the 1970s. And they’ve hit record lows in recent years. While 86% of Americans trusted the American people in 1976, today barely half do.

Adding further nuance to this issue: Gallup also highlights the significant gap between American perceptions of corruption in government (89%) versus corruption in business (71%). The survey says few countries have gaps this large.
And, interestingly, this public perception of corruption does not trickle down to local politics.
In another survey by YouGov many more respondents deemed US senators and representatives to be corrupt (75%) than mid- or low-level government workers (39%).
This gets to an important reason why such high levels of distrust in institutions have not led to more unrest: Americans still appear to have trust in their local governments.

And this has largely not changed since Gallup first polled on the topic more than 50 years ago. Today, two-thirds of Americans trust their local government, which is actually slightly higher than the 63% who did in 1972.
On the whole, Americans also retain trust in the ability of elections – like the midterms – to act as political circuit breakers.
What about the midterms? Candidates running for office this year have taken note of the deep voter distrust in Washington elites, parties and institutions.

One need only watch a few of the many viral political ads this campaign to see a well-worn script: candidates blame Washington insiders for corruption and other issues, while touting their local bona fides.
It should come as no surprise that many candidates are eschewing party labels altogether, often going so far as to criticise their own party.

But this is not the first time politicians of all stripes have appeared keen to distance themselves from the ruling class, and from political insiders viewed as corrupt and detached from the everyday realities of most Americans.

After all, with the exceptions of Biden and George H.W. Bush (both former vice presidents who served under popular two-term presidents), every US president of the last half century has come to the Oval Office with fewer than five years of experience in Washington – if any.
Americans have largely been against Washington insiders for decades – particularly when economic anxiety is high.

title_en: Human speech follows the same patterns as birdsong — new research
excerpt_en: A new study compares the songs of 367 bird species with song and speech from 52 human languages to reveal shared acoustic patterns.
body_en: In every culture, humans speak and sing to each other. We have created an astounding array of languages and musical structures across the globe. And yet, within this diversity, some fundamental sequence patterns are repeated. These are often referred to as “universal” patterns in human vocalization.
Our new research, published this week in Science, reveals that many of these acoustic patterns in human song and speech are also shared with birdsong.
The study compared the songs of 367 bird species with examples of song and speech from 52 human languages.

How we gathered the data As researchers in animal behaviour and neuroscience and music, we ( Logan and Jon) spent 10 years documenting the prevalence of universal human acoustic patterns in the songs of zebra finches.
A zebra finch. (Unsplash/Angelo Casto) When Kendra joined our lab during her PhD, she proposed we investigate whether these patterns are shared across other bird species as well.

To research this, we needed a large number of birdsong recordings. Luckily, many people around the world are fascinated by the sounds of birds and upload their recordings to public repositories. We collected and manually annotated individual syllables in the songs of over 360 bird species, generating more than 70,000 birdsong syllables for analysis.
We then compared these to data sets of human speech and song from a variety of languages and cultures around the world.
Fortunately, some of these data sets contain annotated recordings of the same individual producing both speech and song, which was perfect for our comparisons to bird vocalizations.

Humans and birds both tend to end their phrases with longer syllable. (Unsplash) Regular and predictable rhythms Overall, we found numerous similarities in the acoustic patterns of bird songs and human vocalizations. For example, humans and birds both tend to end their phrases with longer syllables.
Song of a fox sparrow. (Patrik Aberg), CC BY-NC-SA 35 KB (download)
They also organize their syllables in a way that minimizes changes of pitch across adjacent syllables. And they tend to produce their songs with regular and predictable rhythms.
In some cases, birdsong appeared more similar to human song than human speech. In other cases, we found birds tended to have songs that were more similar to human speech than human song.

Unrelated to vocal learning We designed this study to ask an important question: Does vocal learning ability shape sequence patterning? Humans learn the structure of their vocalizations from others, particularly as they grow up.

It turns out many birds also learn their vocalizations as they grow up. We looked at two separate groups of these vocal learning birds: songbirds ( oscines) and hummingbirds. We compared them to two closely related bird groups that are not vocal learners: suboscines and nightjars.

Because humans, songbirds and hummingbirds are all vocal learners, we thought some patterns may be similar within these species and distinct from those within suboscines and nightjars. Surprisingly, we found very little evidence for this. The degree of variation across bird species did not appear to be related to vocal learning.

Yellow-rumped warbler, an oscine songbird. (Unsplash) How humans and birds make sound What then might drive the similarities in sequence patterning across so many species? We will need more studies to determine the answer, but we hypothesize that similarities in how humans and birds produce sounds could shape some vocal sequence patterns.

For example, the shared need to co-ordinate breathing with vocal musculature could contribute to shared acoustic patterning across birds and humans. Specifically, precise movement of muscles that control the vocal tract are timed with airflow from the lungs across all birds and humans.
If this is true, it’s possible these patterns may be found in many other species.

Did birds teach us to sing? Did birdsong influence the evolution of human sound? (Unsplash) Songbirds first evolved about 50 million years ago, long before the first lines of humans split from the other great apes. This means that birds have decorated our soundscapes throughout human evolution.

The songs of birds have inspired music throughout time and cultures. Might these natural sounds have influenced the earliest humans as they began experimenting with making sounds themselves, discovering the joy of music to their ears?
These are some of the big ideas we are excited to explore in future studies.
Logan S. James receives funding from FRQNT. He is affiliated with Earth Species Project and Wavelength Science.
